lessons.title: Black body radiation
lessons.summary: Understand that every object emits and absorbs infrared radiation, what a perfect black body is, how temperature changes the intensity and wavelength of the radiation emitted, and how the balance of radiation sets the temperature of the Earth.
objectives: I can state that all objects emit and absorb infrared radiation, and that hotter objects emit more.
I can explain what is meant by a perfect black body.
I can describe how the intensity and peak wavelength of emitted radiation change with temperature.
I can explain how the rates of absorption and emission determine whether an object's temperature rises, falls or stays constant.
I can explain how the Earth's temperature depends on the balance of radiation absorbed and emitted.

activities.title: Everything glows
activities.content:
## All objects emit and absorb infrared

Hold your hand near (not touching) a radiator and you feel warmth arriving as **infrared radiation**, a part of the electromagnetic spectrum. What is less obvious is that **every object, whatever its temperature, emits infrared radiation**, and every object also **absorbs** infrared that lands on it. You, this screen and an ice cube are all emitting infrared right now.

The **hotter** an object is, the **more infrared radiation it emits every second**. Think of the rate of emission as a measure of temperature: a thermal imaging camera works exactly this way, showing hot objects as bright.

### Good absorbers, good emitters
Surfaces differ in how well they absorb and emit:
- **Dark, matt (dull) surfaces** are **good absorbers and good emitters** of infrared.
- **Light, shiny surfaces** are **poor absorbers and poor emitters**; they reflect most infrared instead.

This is why a black car gets hotter in the sun than a white one, why radiators are (ideally) painted matt, and why survival blankets are shiny to keep body heat in.

Infrared is emitted by everything warm because the particles in the object are vibrating; charged particles that accelerate emit electromagnetic waves.

question.text: Which of these objects emits infrared radiation?
question.hint: Every object above absolute zero emits infrared, not just hot ones.
question.explanation: All objects emit infrared radiation, whatever their temperature. A hot object emits more per second than a cold one, but even ice emits some.

options.text: All of them
Only the cup of hot tea
options.feedback: Cool objects emit less, but they still emit.

options.text: The cup of tea and the person, but not the ice cube
None of them, only the Sun emits infrared

activities.title: The perfect black body
activities.content:
## What is a black body?

Scientists define an ideal object to compare real ones against. A **perfect black body** is an object that:

- **absorbs all** the radiation that falls on it, at every wavelength, and
- **reflects or transmits none** of it.

Because it absorbs everything, a perfect black body would look completely black at room temperature. But it is also the **best possible emitter** of radiation: a good absorber is always a good emitter. When it is hot, a black body glows brightly.

No real object is a perfect black body, but some come close:
- a small hole in a hollow box (radiation entering bounces around inside and is absorbed before it can escape),
- **stars** such as the Sun, whose spectra are very close to black-body spectra,
- black soot.

The radiation emitted by a black body is called **black body radiation**, and it depends on **only one thing: the temperature** of the body. Two black bodies at the same temperature emit exactly the same spectrum, whatever they are made of.

A black body does not emit at a single wavelength. It emits a **continuous range of wavelengths**, with different amounts at each wavelength. The shape of that distribution is what changes with temperature.

question.text: Complete the definition of a perfect black body.

metadata.blanksText: A perfect black body ___ all the radiation that falls on it and does not ___ or transmit any.

question.hint: The two words are opposites in a sense: taking radiation in versus bouncing it back.
question.explanation: A perfect black body absorbs all incident radiation and reflects or transmits none. It is also the best possible emitter.

activities.title: How temperature changes the radiation
activities.content:
## Intensity and wavelength

Heat a piece of iron in a forge. At first you feel it emitting infrared but see nothing. As it gets hotter it glows dull red, then orange, then yellow, and a very hot piece glows white. Two things are happening.

### 1. The intensity increases
**Intensity** is the power radiated per square metre of surface. As the temperature rises, the object emits **more radiation at every wavelength**, so the total intensity goes up steeply. (Doubling the absolute temperature multiplies the power by 16, though you do not need that number.)

### 2. The peak wavelength gets shorter
The emitted radiation is spread over a range of wavelengths with a **peak** at one particular wavelength. As temperature rises, this **peak shifts to shorter wavelengths** (higher frequencies):

| Object | Temperature | Peak wavelength | Appearance |
|---|---|---|---|
| Human body | 37 °C (310 K) | about 10 μm (infrared) | invisible glow |
| Electric hob | 700 K | far red / infrared | dull red |
| Light bulb filament | 3000 K | near infrared, some visible | yellow-white |
| Sun's surface | 5800 K | 0.5 μm (green-yellow, visible) | white |
| Blue-white star | 20 000 K | ultraviolet | blue-white |

```
Intensity
   |      hot: taller peak, further left
   |     /\
   |    /  \__       cool: low, broad, peak to the right
   |   /   ___\_____
   |  /  _/        \_______
   |_/__/______________________ Wavelength
    short                   long
```

A hotter body's curve is **higher everywhere** and its **peak is further to the left** (shorter wavelength). This is why astronomers can find a star's surface temperature just from its colour.

question.text: Two stars, A and B, both behave as black bodies. Star A is hotter than star B. Which TWO statements are correct?
question.hint: Hotter means more radiation and a peak at shorter wavelength.
question.explanation: The hotter star emits more radiation per square metre at every wavelength, and its intensity peak is at a shorter wavelength. It does not emit at only one wavelength, and its peak is not at a longer wavelength.

options.text: Star A emits more radiation per square metre of surface than star B
The peak of star A's emission is at a shorter wavelength than star B's
Star A emits radiation at only one wavelength
options.feedback: Black bodies emit a continuous range of wavelengths.

options.text: Star A's peak wavelength is longer than star B's

question.text: Place these glowing objects in order of INCREASING temperature (coolest first), based on the colour they emit.
question.hint: Red is the longest visible wavelength, so a red glow means the lowest temperature of the four.
question.explanation: As temperature rises the peak wavelength shortens: red → orange/yellow → white → blue-white.

activities.title: Absorbing versus emitting
activities.content:
## What decides whether an object warms up or cools down?

Every object is doing two things at once: **absorbing** radiation from its surroundings and **emitting** its own. Its temperature depends on the **balance** between them.

- If it **absorbs more than it emits**, its temperature **rises**.
- If it **emits more than it absorbs**, its temperature **falls**.
- If it **absorbs and emits at the same rate**, its temperature stays **constant**. This is called being in **equilibrium**.

### An everyday example
Take a mug of hot coffee into a cool room. The coffee emits infrared quickly (it is hot) and absorbs only a little from the cooler surroundings, so it cools. As it cools its emission rate drops. Eventually it emits at the same rate it absorbs and its temperature settles at room temperature.

### A cold object
A cold can taken from the fridge absorbs more radiation from the warm room than it emits, so it warms up until, again, the two rates match.

### Not just radiation
In practice objects also exchange energy by **conduction** and **convection**. But for anything in space, or anything separated from its surroundings by a vacuum (a vacuum flask), **radiation is the only way** energy can get in or out. That makes the balance of radiation absorbed and emitted the whole story for planets and stars.

activities.title: Worked example: the temperature of a planet
activities.content:
**Why does the Earth stay at a roughly steady average temperature?**

The Earth receives radiation from the Sun at a steady rate (mostly visible and near-infrared, because the Sun's surface is at about 5800 K).

- Some of this is **reflected** back into space by clouds, ice and the atmosphere. About 30 % is reflected in total.
- The rest is **absorbed** by the ground, oceans and air, warming them.
- The warm Earth **emits** its own radiation. At about 288 K (15 °C), this peaks in the infrared at roughly 10 μm.

The Earth's temperature settles at the value where the **rate of infrared emitted equals the rate of solar radiation absorbed**. If the Earth warmed slightly, it would emit more and cool back; if it cooled, it would emit less and warm back. That is a stable equilibrium.

**During the day** a patch of ground absorbs more than it emits, so it warms up. **At night** there is no incoming sunlight; it emits more than it absorbs, so it cools. Clear nights are colder than cloudy ones because clouds absorb some of the outgoing infrared and re-emit part of it back down.

**Greenhouse gases** (carbon dioxide, methane, water vapour) also absorb outgoing infrared and re-emit it in all directions, including downwards. This raises the temperature at which the Earth reaches balance. More greenhouse gas means a higher equilibrium temperature, which is the physics behind global warming.

question.text: True or false: an object whose temperature is staying constant must not be emitting any radiation.
question.hint: Can an object be absorbing and emitting at the same time?
question.explanation: False. All objects emit radiation constantly. A constant temperature means the object is emitting at the same rate as it is absorbing, so the two balance.

options.text: True
False

question.text: A metal bench has been in the sun all day. After sunset its temperature falls. Explain why, in terms of radiation absorbed and emitted.
question.hint: Compare the rate the bench absorbs radiation with the rate it emits after the Sun goes down.
question.explanation: After sunset the bench absorbs much less radiation because the Sun is no longer shining on it, but it continues to emit infrared because it is warm. It now emits more than it absorbs, so its temperature falls.

markScheme.criterion: After sunset the bench absorbs less radiation / no longer receives radiation from the Sun
It emits more than it absorbs so its temperature decreases

question.text:
The Sun can be treated as a perfect black body with a surface temperature of about 5800 K. A cooler star has a surface temperature of about 3500 K.

(a) State what is meant by a perfect black body. (2 marks)

(b) Describe TWO differences between the radiation emitted by the Sun and by the cooler star. (2 marks)

(c) Explain why the surface temperature of the cooler star stays constant. (1 mark)
question.hint: For (b), think about the total intensity and where the peak of the spectrum lies.
question.explanation: (a) An object that absorbs all the radiation incident on it, reflecting and transmitting none; it is also the best possible emitter. (b) The Sun emits a greater intensity at every wavelength / more radiation per second per square metre, and its peak is at a shorter wavelength (visible) while the cooler star's peak is at a longer wavelength (red/infrared). (c) The star emits radiation at the same rate as energy is supplied to its surface from inside (or absorbed), so it is in equilibrium.

markScheme.criterion: Absorbs all radiation that falls on it
Reflects / transmits none, or is the best possible emitter
Sun emits more radiation / higher intensity at every wavelength
Sun's peak is at a shorter wavelength / higher frequency than the cooler star's
Rate of emission equals rate of energy supplied / absorbed (equilibrium)

activities.title: Key points
activities.content:
- **All objects emit and absorb infrared radiation.** The hotter the object, the more it emits per second.
- Dark matt surfaces are good absorbers and emitters; light shiny surfaces are poor absorbers and emitters.
- A **perfect black body** absorbs **all** radiation that hits it, reflecting and transmitting none, and is the **best possible emitter**.
- As temperature rises, the emitted radiation's **intensity increases** at every wavelength and the **peak moves to shorter wavelengths** (red → white → blue).
- Temperature **rises** if absorption > emission, **falls** if emission > absorption, and is **constant** when the two rates are equal.
- The Earth's temperature is set by the balance between solar radiation absorbed and infrared emitted; greenhouse gases shift that balance to a higher temperature.

practiceQuestions.text: True or false: only objects that are hotter than their surroundings emit infrared radiation.
practiceQuestions.hint: Think about whether a cold object still emits.
practiceQuestions.explanation: False. All objects emit infrared regardless of their temperature; hotter objects simply emit more.

options.text: True
False

practiceQuestions.text: Which surface is the best emitter of infrared radiation?
practiceQuestions.explanation: Dark, matt surfaces are the best absorbers and therefore the best emitters. Shiny surfaces reflect infrared and emit poorly.

options.text: Matt black
Shiny silver
Glossy white
Polished gold

metadata.blanksText: As the temperature of a black body increases, the intensity of the radiation it emits ___ and the wavelength at which the peak occurs becomes ___.

practiceQuestions.hint: Think about a heating element going from dull red to white.
practiceQuestions.explanation: Higher temperature: greater intensity and a shorter peak wavelength.

practiceQuestions.text: A star appears blue-white while another appears red. What can you conclude?
practiceQuestions.hint: Blue light has a shorter wavelength than red.
practiceQuestions.explanation: The blue-white star's peak emission is at a shorter wavelength, so it has a higher surface temperature than the red star.

options.text: The blue-white star has a higher surface temperature
The red star has a higher surface temperature
Both stars have the same temperature but different sizes
The red star emits no infrared

practiceQuestions.text: Match each situation to what happens to the object's temperature.
practiceQuestions.hint: Compare the rate of absorption with the rate of emission.
practiceQuestions.explanation: Absorbing more than emitting warms an object; emitting more than absorbing cools it; equal rates give a constant temperature.

pairs.left: Absorbs radiation faster than it emits
Emits radiation faster than it absorbs
Absorbs and emits at the same rate

practiceQuestions.text: Which TWO of the following are properties of a perfect black body?
practiceQuestions.explanation: A perfect black body absorbs all incident radiation and is the best possible emitter. It reflects nothing and emits a continuous spectrum, not a single wavelength.

options.text: It absorbs all the radiation incident on it
It is the best possible emitter of radiation
It reflects all radiation incident on it
It emits radiation at only one wavelength

practiceQuestions.text: The Earth absorbs solar radiation at an average rate of 240 W for each square metre of its surface. For its temperature to remain constant, at what average rate, in W/m², must it emit infrared radiation?
practiceQuestions.hint: Constant temperature means absorption rate equals emission rate.
practiceQuestions.explanation: For a steady temperature, emission must equal absorption: 240 W/m².

practiceQuestions.text: Explain why a clear night is usually colder than a cloudy night.
practiceQuestions.hint: Clouds interact with the infrared that the ground emits.
practiceQuestions.explanation: The ground emits infrared radiation at night. On a clear night this escapes into space, so the ground emits more than it absorbs and cools quickly. Clouds absorb some of the outgoing infrared and re-emit part of it back to the ground, reducing the net loss.

markScheme.criterion: The ground emits infrared at night which escapes to space when there are no clouds
Clouds absorb / reflect the infrared and re-emit some back down, so less net energy is lost

practiceQuestions.text:
The amount of carbon dioxide in the Earth's atmosphere has increased over the last century.

(a) Describe how the Earth's average temperature is normally kept constant in terms of radiation. (2 marks)

(b) Explain how an increase in carbon dioxide can lead to an increase in the Earth's average temperature. (2 marks)
practiceQuestions.hint: For (b), carbon dioxide absorbs infrared but lets visible sunlight through.
practiceQuestions.explanation: (a) The Earth absorbs radiation from the Sun and emits infrared radiation; the temperature is steady when the rate of emission to space equals the rate of absorption. (b) Carbon dioxide absorbs some of the infrared emitted by the Earth and re-emits it in all directions, including back towards the surface. Less energy escapes to space, so the Earth absorbs more than it emits and warms until a new, higher balance is reached.

markScheme.criterion: Earth absorbs radiation from the Sun and emits infrared radiation
Temperature is constant when the rate of emission equals the rate of absorption
Carbon dioxide absorbs infrared emitted by the Earth / re-emits some back to the surface
Less radiation escapes so absorption exceeds emission and temperature rises until a new balance
